transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, my parents kind of pushed me to make this appointment, but I guess I know I need to be here. I'm taking some college classes right now—not working or anything, just trying to focus on school—but things have gotten really, really out of hand lately. It's just... it's about food, mostly. Or, well, my relationship with it. 

I came in because... it's like, once I start eating, I just completely lose my grip on everything. It's honestly the scariest feeling. It feels like I just disappear, you know? Like my actual self just checks out and something else entirely takes over my body. And the crazy part is, I'm still in there somewhere, like in the back of my head, practically screaming at myself to just put the food down, just stop chewing, just walk away from the kitchen. But I can't. I just keep going and going, even while I'm telling myself to stop, until I physically can't stand it anymore and I feel like I'm going to burst. It's just taking up so much of my time and energy, and it's ruining my focus for my classes and my whole life, really, because I just have absolutely zero power to stop it once it starts...
Do you ever make yourself vomit or do something else to try to get rid of the food after one of these eating episodes?

Yeah... yeah, I do. I mean, I feel like I almost have to. The second I finally snap out of it and stop eating, this massive, suffocating wave of panic just hits me. It's like this ticking clock in my head. I can physically feel all that food just... sitting right there in my stomach, and I get so absolutely terrified that it's just sitting there turning into weight. Like, every single second I waste, it's just absorbing and making me bigger. It's honestly sheer terror. 

So, I usually end up rushing to a bathroom somewhere to make myself throw up. If I'm in my dorm, I have to kind of sneak around and make sure my roommate isn't around, or I try to wait until the communal bathroom is empty, which is super stressful because I'm racing against the clock. But a lot of times, I'll go to the library. There's this really quiet floor near the top where the older books are, and the bathroom there is almost always completely empty. I just go in there and get rid of it. I hate sneaking around campus like that, constantly worrying if someone's going to walk in and hear me, but I just can't handle the thought of all those calories staying inside me. The anxiety is just so intense, I literally can't focus on my homework or anything else until I've gone to the bathroom and undone it...
How often do these episodes of eating and then purging happen?

God, it's... it's a lot. If I really sit down and think about it, like, for most of this semester... it's been happening several times a week. It's definitely not just a once-in-a-while thing anymore, even though I keep trying to convince myself it is. 

I keep telling myself, like, okay, this Monday is going to be a totally fresh start. I'll wake up, I'll go to my morning lectures, I'll eat a normal lunch in the dining hall, and I just won't do it. I'll be normal. But then Tuesday hits, or maybe Wednesday, and the stress just builds up or I get triggered by something stupid, and I totally cave. And then once I do it that first time, it's like the seal is completely broken for the rest of the week, and I end up doing it again the next day, and then maybe the day after that. 

I was actually looking at the calendar on my phone the other day, just trying to figure out when it got this bad, and I can look back over at least the last few months—basically since the semester really got going and the workload piled up—and there really hasn't been a single week where the cycle stopped. Not one. I just keep repeating the same exact pattern, over and over, multiple days a week, and it's so exhausting trying to keep track of it all and hide it from my roommate for that many days in a row. Like, you'd think I'd get a break for just seven days, just one normal week where I don't end up hunched over in that library bathroom trying to be quiet, but no. It just never stops.
Do you exercise to try to burn off calories after one of these episodes?

No, I don't really do that. I mean, I know some people probably do, like go for a run or hit the gym or whatever, but I just... I don't. Honestly, by the time the whole thing is over—like, after I've eaten all that food and then rushed to the bathroom to get rid of it—I am just completely wiped out. It's like my whole body just feels heavy and drained, you know? 

And on top of that, I'm just so focused on my classes right now. Or, well, I'm trying to be focused on my classes. Between the studying and the reading and just trying to keep my head above water with my coursework, and then dealing with this whole... cycle... taking up so much of my mental energy and time, I just can't imagine trying to fit in a workout on top of it all. I don't even really like exercising anyway, to be completely honest. I've never been the athletic type, not in high school, not now. So, no, I don't go to the campus gym or run around the quad or anything like that. The throwing up is really the only thing I do to try and fix it, because the panic is just so immediate, I need it gone right then and there. I couldn't handle waiting to burn it off even if I wanted to, which I don't. So yeah, just the throwing up. No exercise.
Do you think you are currently underweight, overweight, or at a normal weight?

I mean... I guess I'm probably at a normal weight? At least, that's what the scale says most of the time, but it's so hard to really trust it, you know? Like, I step on it and I see the number, and logically I know it falls into whatever the normal range is supposed to be for a guy my height, but when I look in the mirror, it just doesn't feel true. It feels like a lie. 

I constantly feel like I'm heavy, or like I'm just right on the edge of getting fat. Like, if I mess up even a little bit, if I don't get rid of the food fast enough, I'm just going to balloon up overnight. I spend so much time just staring at myself, pulling at my shirts to make sure they aren't clinging to my stomach, comparing myself to the other guys in my dorm who all seem to just effortlessly look fit and normal without even trying. It's exhausting. 

So, yeah, officially, I guess I'm normal weight, but I definitely don't feel normal. I don't feel like I fit in that category. I just feel like this bloated, heavy mess all the time, and I'm terrified that one day the scale is going to finally catch up to how I actually feel inside. It's like I'm just faking being a normal weight, and the throwing up is the only thing keeping the illusion going. I don't know... it's just really messed up how my brain sees it versus what the actual number is.
Is the fear of gaining weight something that is always on your mind, even when you're not in the middle of one of these eating episodes?

Yeah, it really is. It’s... it’s honestly like a hum in the background of everything I do, all day long. Like, I can be having a completely normal day, you know? I’ll go to my morning classes, take my notes, maybe even feel pretty good about a quiz I just took or something. I’ll be having a decent day. But then... I don't know, I’ll be walking across campus, and I’ll just catch my reflection in the glass of one of the dorm windows, or even just in the mirror in the bathroom between classes. And if I look at myself and think my stomach looks even slightly bigger, or my face looks rounder than the other guys around me... it just ruins everything. 

It’s like this instant, crushing weight. Suddenly, the fact that I did well on a quiz doesn't matter at all. It feels like I’ve just failed at everything, like my whole worth is tied up in how I look in that one second. And when that happens, I just... I don’t want anyone to see me. I want to pull my hoodie down, cross my arms over my stomach, and just disappear. I’ll start analyzing every single thing I ate that day, or what I ate the day before, and I’ll start comparing myself to literally every guy I walk past on the sidewalk. Like, 'Oh, his jawline is sharper than mine,' or 'His shirt fits him perfectly and mine is clinging to my sides.' 

It’s so exhausting because I can’t just turn it off. Even when I’m sitting in a lecture hall, trying to focus on what the professor is saying, half my brain is thinking about how I’m sitting and if my posture is making my stomach roll, or if the person sitting next to me is judging how much space I’m taking up. It’s not just when I’m eating or throwing up. It’s literally all the time. It dictates what clothes I choose in the morning, where I sit in the dining hall, whether I even want to hang out with my friends on the weekend. If I feel 'fat' that day, I just won't go out. I’ll make up an excuse about having too much homework because the thought of people looking at me and thinking I’ve gained weight is just... I can't handle it. So, yeah, it's definitely always there. Always.
Do you think your worth as a person is tied to your weight or appearance?

I mean... yeah. Yeah, I really do. I know it sounds messed up when I say it out loud, but it's like... it's exactly what I was just saying about the window reflection, you know? Like, I could literally be having the best day. I could ace a midterm, I could get a compliment from a professor, I could be feeling like I actually belong in college and I'm doing a good job. I can have a decent day in classes, and I'll feel smart, I'll feel capable. But then... if I catch my reflection in a dorm window, or just pass by a mirror in the student union, and I think my stomach looks even a little bit bigger, or my face looks rounder or puffier than the guys around me... it all just evaporates.

It literally feels like I failed at everything. The good grades don't matter. Being a good student doesn't matter. Being a good friend doesn't matter. All that matters in that split second is that I look wrong, and therefore I am wrong. It's this overwhelming sense of... of worthlessness, really. I just don't want anyone to see me. I want to hide in my room and not come out because I feel like everyone else is looking at me and thinking the exact same things I'm thinking about myself. They're thinking I'm heavy, or lazy, or whatever. 

It's like my entire value as a human being is completely dependent on whether my stomach is flat that day. And if it's not, then I'm nothing. I'm just a failure. And I hate that I think that way, I really do, because logically I know there's more to me than my body. I know I have a brain, I know I'm trying hard in school. But none of that logic stands a chance when I feel fat. The feeling just completely takes over and tells me that if I don't look perfect, I don't deserve to feel good about anything else in my life. So yeah... my weight is basically the only thing that dictates how I feel about myself on any given day.
Is your fear of gaining weight the main reason you make yourself vomit after eating?

Yeah... yeah, it absolutely is. It’s the only reason, really. Because when I have one of those moments where I just eat and eat... the panic that sets in right after is just, it's indescribable. It's like this overwhelming, suffocating terror. I can physically feel the food inside me, feeling so heavy and wrong, and my brain just starts screaming at me. Like, I can literally picture the food just sitting there in my stomach, turning into weight, turning into fat, right that very second. 

And I can't handle that thought. I just can't sit with it. So, after I eat like that, I usually end up rushing to find a bathroom so I can make myself throw up. If I'm back at my building, I'll use the dorm bathroom, but I always have to pace around and check if the guys on my hall are hanging out nearby, which is a whole other stressful thing because the walls are so thin. Or, a lot of times, I'll go up to a quiet floor of the library. You know, like the upper floors where the old reference books are and no one really goes unless it's finals week? There's a bathroom tucked away in the corner up there that's almost always empty. 

I'll just lock myself in a stall and make myself throw up, just to get it out. Because I am just so terrified that if I don't, the food is just sitting there turning into weight. It’s like a race against the clock in my head. If I don't get rid of it fast enough, it's going to be permanent, and I'll wake up the next day completely bloated and huge, and everyone will be able to tell. So the fear of that happening... yeah, that's exactly why I do it. I just have to stop the food from staying inside me.
Do you feel like you have no control over what you're eating or how much you're eating during these episodes?

Yeah, exactly. That's actually a huge part of why I finally decided to come in and talk to someone. Because it's not just like, "Oh, I was really hungry and I ate a big meal." It's so much scarier than that. It’s like... once I take that first bite, if I'm in my dorm late at night and my roommate is out, and I open a bag of chips or something, it's like I just disappear. 

The rational part of my brain, the part that cares about my weight and my classes and everything we were just talking about, it just gets pushed aside. It feels like something else completely takes over my body. I'll be sitting there on my bed, cramming food into my mouth, and in my head, I'm literally screaming at myself. I'm thinking, "What are you doing? Stop! You're going to regret this so much, you're going to have to go throw this up, just put the bag down!" But my hands just keep moving. It's like I'm a passenger in my own body watching someone else do it. 

I'll go through the chips, then I'll find a box of cereal, then maybe some stale cookies I have shoved in my desk drawer, or I'll even go down to the vending machine in the lobby and buy four or five candy bars. I don't even taste it half the time. I'm not eating because it tastes good. I just keep chewing and swallowing and opening new wrappers, and I keep going and going until I physically cannot fit another bite into my stomach. I literally don't stop until it hurts so bad I can't even stand up straight, until I just can't stand it anymore. 

And the whole time, I'm so aware of how messed up it is, but I have absolutely zero power to stop it. It’s like a trance. I can't control what I'm grabbing, I can't control how fast I'm eating... it's just this frantic, desperate feeling. That total loss of control is just... it's terrifying. It makes me feel completely crazy, honestly, because I know I don't want to be doing it, but I just can't make myself stop.
Do you usually feel guilty or ashamed after one of these eating episodes, before you make yourself vomit?

I mean... I don't know if guilt is really the right word for that specific moment. Like, I'm not sure I've ever really stopped to notice if I feel ashamed right then, because... well, the second I stop eating, when I literally can't take another bite, there isn't really room in my head for guilt. It's just pure, absolute panic. 

Like I was saying before, it's a race against the clock. So I'm not sitting on my bed thinking, "Oh, I'm such a bad person, I'm so ashamed of myself." I don't have time for that. My brain just immediately shifts into this emergency override mode. I'll be looking at the empty wrappers—the chip bags, the candy wrappers, the cereal box, whatever is just scattered all over my bed—and I don't really feel guilty looking at them. I just feel completely terrified of what they represent, you know? It's like, I have to get this out of me *now*. 

I'll be grabbing my dorm keys, shoving the wrappers under my pillow so my roommate doesn't see them if he walks in, and then I'm cracking my door open to check the hallway. I'm listening to see if the guys next door are playing video games with their door open, or if anyone is walking up the stairs. And my heart is just pounding so hard I can actually hear it in my ears, and I'm usually sweating and kind of shaking. 

So if you're asking if I sit there and feel ashamed before I go to the bathroom... I really don't think so. I haven't noticed feeling that way. It's just this frantic, tunnel-vision need to fix what I just did. Maybe the shame comes later, like way later when I'm finally back in my room and I'm trying to fall asleep and my throat hurts and I'm just so exhausted... but right in that gap between the eating and getting to the bathroom? No, I don't think I feel guilty then. I'm just way too scared.
Do you make yourself vomit after these eating episodes specifically because you're afraid of gaining weight from the food you've eaten?

Well, yeah... I mean, I think I just said that, but yes, absolutely. It's... it's the entire reason. Like I was saying, after one of those times where I just lose control and eat everything in sight, I usually end up in a bathroom somewhere, either in the dorm if I can sneak past the guys on my hall, or up on one of those quiet floors in the library where no one goes. And I make myself throw up because... well, because I am just so completely terrified that the food is just sitting there inside me, literally turning into weight right then and there. 

It's like I can feel it happening, you know? Like this heavy, horrible feeling in my stomach, and my brain is just screaming that if I don't get it out right that second, it's going to stick to me and I'll be huge. So, yeah, I make myself sick because I'm just so incredibly scared of gaining weight from all that food. It's the only way I can make that panic stop, the only way I can feel like I've undone the damage, even though I know it's messed up. I just can't handle the thought of that food staying inside me.
Is the fear of gaining weight the only reason you purge after eating, or is it also because you feel like you've lost control over how much you've eaten?

I mean... I don't really know. Like, I haven't really thought about it like that, splitting it up into different reasons, you know? It's all just kind of this one huge, awful mess in my head. 

I guess... I mean, I know I just talked about the weight thing, and that's huge, obviously. That's the main thing I'm focused on when I'm in that panic mode. But the control part... I don't know. Maybe? Because, like I was explaining before, the feeling of losing control when I'm eating is just so terrifying. It's like I'm watching myself do something I hate, and I can't stop it. So maybe throwing up is... I don't know, maybe it is a way to get some of that control back? Like, my body did this thing I didn't want it to do, it ate all this food, and now I'm forcing it to undo it. 

But honestly, in that moment, when I'm rushing to the bathroom and trying not to be seen by the guys in my hall, I'm not really analyzing my motivations like that. I'm not sitting there thinking, "Ah yes, I am purging to regain a sense of autonomy." I'm just thinking, "Get it out, get it out, get it out." 

So I don't really know if the loss of control is a separate reason for doing it, or if it's just all tied up in the fear of the weight. It's like... the loss of control leads to the food, the food leads to the fear of weight, and the fear of weight leads to the bathroom. It's just this one continuous loop. I'm sorry, I know that's probably not a very helpful answer. I just... I haven't really dissected it like that before. It's all just this one big, desperate reaction, you know?
When you make yourself vomit after one of these episodes, is it specifically to undo the calories you've just consumed?

Well, yeah, I mean... exactly. That's exactly it. It's all about the calories, the food, the weight... it's like this math equation in my head that I just have to balance out. I know I keep saying this, and I feel like I'm repeating myself, but it really is just that simple and that complicated all at once. 

When I have one of those episodes where I just completely lose it and eat everything... like I was saying before, I usually end up sprinting to a bathroom. Either the one at the end of my hall if I think I can make it without running into my roommate or the guys next door, or I'll literally hike all the way across campus to the library. There's this one bathroom on the top floor, way in the back past the old bound periodicals, where nobody ever goes. I've spent so much time in that specific stall. I know exactly which tile is loose on the floor. 

And I'm in there, making myself throw up, because... because I am just so absolutely terrified that all those calories, all that food I just shoved down my throat, is just sitting right there in my stomach. It feels like a rock. And in my head, I'm picturing it literally turning into fat, into weight, right in that exact moment. Like if I wait even five minutes, it's too late, the calories are already absorbed, the damage is done. 

So, yeah, it's specifically to undo the calories. It's like... if I can just get it all out, if I can just empty my stomach completely, then it's like it never happened. The calories don't count if they don't stay inside me, right? That's the logic my brain uses, anyway. Even though my throat is burning and my eyes are watering and I feel like absolute garbage, the only thing that matters is getting those calories out before they can stick to me. It's the only way I can breathe again.
Do you ever restrict your food intake to the point of significant weight loss or severe nutritional deficiency?

I mean, no, not really. Not like... not like starving myself or anything like that. I don't think I've ever lost a bunch of weight all at once, or, you know, gotten sick from not eating enough vitamins or whatever you mean by nutritional deficiency. 

It's actually kind of the opposite problem, right? Like, I'm eating so much during those times when I lose control. But then, obviously, I'm trying to get rid of it. But in between all that... I do try to restrict what I eat, I really do. Like, I'll wake up after a bad night, after spending an hour in that library bathroom I told you about, and I'll just be so disgusted with myself. I'll look in the mirror in my dorm room—well, I try not to look, honestly, because I just hate what I see—but I'll tell myself, "Okay, today is the day. Today I'm only going to have black coffee and maybe an apple. I'm going to be perfectly controlled." 

And I'll try. I'll go to the dining hall and just get a salad with no dressing, and I'll sit there watching all the other guys on my floor eating burgers and fries, and it's just... it's torture. It's like my brain is just constantly buzzing with thoughts about food. I'll make it through the morning, maybe even the afternoon, just drinking water and trying to ignore how empty my stomach feels. But it never lasts long enough to actually make me lose weight or get deficient in anything. Because eventually, the hunger just gets too loud, or I get stressed about a paper, or I just feel so lonely and miserable, and then... then the whole cycle starts over again. I end up back in my room with a massive pile of food from the vending machines or the convenience store down the street. 

So, yeah, I try to restrict, I really try to be strict with myself to make up for the bad times, but I always end up failing. I never actually get to the point where I'm losing significant weight from it because the bingeing always ruins it. It's just this constant, exhausting back-and-forth, and my weight just kind of stays around the same, which honestly just makes me feel even worse because I feel like I'm doing all this awful stuff to my body and I'm not even getting the result I want, you know? It's just a mess.
Do you ever experience a period of time where you don't binge eat or purge, but instead severely restrict your food intake for several days or weeks?

I mean... days or weeks? No. Definitely not. I wish I could, honestly, but no, I've never made it anywhere near that long. 

Like I was just saying a minute ago, I try to restrict. I really, really try. I'll make all these elaborate plans in my head. I'll even write it down in my planner sometimes, right next to my assignment due dates, like, "Monday: water only. Tuesday: one apple and black coffee." I build it up in my head like I'm finally going to take control, like I'm going to go on this long fast and completely reset my body and finally be disciplined. 

But it never, ever lasts for days. I think the absolute longest I've ever made it was maybe... I don't know, maybe 36 hours? And that was only because I had a massive history paper due and I basically locked myself in the library and drank about six energy drinks and just rode the caffeine anxiety until I crashed. But usually? I can barely make it 24 hours. 

It's just... the pressure builds up way too fast. I'll get to the evening of day one, and I'll be sitting in my dorm, trying to read for my intro to psych class or whatever, and the hunger just turns into this deafening static in my head. I can't focus on the words on the page. I can't watch a video. I can't even hold a normal conversation with my roommate because all I'm thinking about is the fact that I'm not eating, and then suddenly, all I can think about is everything I *want* to eat. 

It's like a pressure cooker, you know? I try to lock the lid down tight and tell myself I'm going to starve for a week, but the steam just builds and builds until I completely snap. By Monday night, I'm just pacing the room, listening to my roommate breathe while he sleeps, just waiting for the coast to be clear so I can sneak down to the vending machines in the basement or walk over to the 24-hour convenience store. 

So, no, I don't have these long stretches where I'm just severely restricting. I wish I had that kind of willpower, as messed up as that sounds. For me, the restricting is really just... it's just the waiting period between the binges. It's just the setup for the next failure. It never lasts more than a day or so before the whole awful cycle just explodes all over again.
Is getting rid of the calories from the food you ate the primary reason you make yourself vomit after these episodes?

Yeah, exactly. I know I kind of just went on a whole tangent about this a few minutes ago, but... yeah, that is absolutely the primary reason. It's the only reason, really. 

After I eat like that, when I've just totally lost all control and eaten everything in sight, I usually end up practically running to a bathroom—either the shared one in my dorm, if I can manage to sneak in without my roommate or any of the guys on my floor seeing me, or, you know, up on that super quiet floor of the library I was telling you about. I just have to get somewhere isolated as fast as humanly possible. 

And I'm in there making myself throw up purely because I feel... I just feel so completely terrified that the food is just sitting there. Like, I can physically feel it just sitting in my stomach like a massive, heavy brick, and my brain is just screaming at me that it's instantly turning into weight. It's this absolute, blinding panic that every second I wait, another calorie is being absorbed, and it's just attaching to my body and making me bigger. So getting rid of it, getting those calories out before they can actually turn into fat and change how I look... that's the whole point of doing it. It's the only thing that makes that terrified feeling stop.
Do you currently have, or have you ever had, a period of time where you maintained a significantly low body weight for an extended period?

No, never. And honestly, that’s the part that just... it drives me completely crazy. Like, I’ve never been significantly low weight, not ever. I’ve always just been... average. Or at least, I feel like I'm massive, but I guess on paper I'm just normal. When I was in middle school and early high school, I was maybe a little chubby, which I absolutely hated, and I thought when I came to college and started... well, doing all this, that I would finally get really thin. But it just hasn't happened. 

I actually have this digital scale that I bought at Target the second week of freshman year, and I keep it shoved way back under my bed in its original box so my roommate doesn't see it. I pull it out, like, every single morning when he goes to his 8 AM calc class. I strip down to nothing, make sure I've gone to the bathroom first, and I stand on it, just praying the number will be drastically lower. But it just... it just hovers right around the exact same five-pound range. It never drops into anything you'd call "significantly low." 

It’s so incredibly frustrating because I feel like I’m putting my body through a literal warzone, right? With the eating all that junk and then the panic and the throwing up in the library and then trying to starve myself the next day... you’d think—or at least I thought—that I’d have something to show for it. Like I’d be one of those guys who just looks incredibly lean and sharp, where my clothes just hang off me. But my jeans fit exactly the same as they did when my parents dropped me off in August. Sometimes they even feel tighter after a bad weekend, which just sends me into a total spiral of panic. 

So, no, I’ve never maintained a low weight. Not for a week, not for a month, never. My body just aggressively fights to stay right in the middle, which honestly makes me feel like such a massive failure. Like I can't even do this right. I'm doing all these extreme things, spending all my money on vending machine food, ruining my throat, and I just look like a completely regular, average guy to everyone else on campus. They have no idea what I'm doing behind closed doors because I don't look sick. It's like a sick joke, honestly. So yeah, definitely no extended periods of being really low weight. I wish, but no.
Do you feel like you would still make yourself vomit after eating even if you weren't afraid of gaining weight?

I mean... no. I really don't think so. Honestly, I can't even wrap my head around that scenario because the fear of gaining weight is literally the entire reason I do it. Like, if I wasn't terrified of getting bigger, why on earth would I put myself through all of that? 

Making yourself throw up is completely miserable. It's not like it's a fun time, you know? My throat always burns afterward, my eyes get all puffy and bloodshot, and I constantly have this low-grade, nagging anxiety that someone in the dorm is going to hear me gagging or smell it on my breath when I walk back into my room. It's disgusting and it's so physically exhausting. 

If I could just eat whatever I wanted, like if I could just sit in the dining hall and eat five bowls of cereal and a whole pizza and know for an absolute fact that I wouldn't gain a single ounce... man, I would never go near a toilet again. I would just eat and then go back to my room and hang out or go to sleep like a normal person. 

The only reason I'm ever in that bathroom stall, practically suffocating myself to get everything up, is because the thought of my jeans not fitting or stepping on that digital scale under my bed and seeing the number go up by even half a pound just completely paralyzes me. Like I was saying before, the panic is entirely about the food turning into fat. It's not about anything else. If you somehow took that fear away, if I just magically didn't care what I looked like or how much I weighed, the throwing up would stop instantly. There just wouldn't be any point to it anymore. So, no, definitely not. It is one hundred percent about the weight.
Do you typically feel a significant sense of relief after purging, which motivates you to continue this behavior?

Relief? I mean... I'm not really sure if 'relief' is the right word for it. And I definitely don't know if I'd say it's what motivates me to keep doing it. 

Like, I guess the immediate, blinding panic that I was talking about before—the fear of the calories—that part stops. But I wouldn't call what's left over a significant sense of relief. It's more like... well, let me just explain what happens right after, because it's really hard to put into words unless you're in it. 

When I finally finish up in that library bathroom, I'm usually kneeling there on these disgusting, freezing floor tiles, and my knees are aching, and my heart is just pounding out of my chest. I flush the toilet, usually like three or four times just to be absolutely, paranoid-level sure every single trace is gone so the janitor or whoever doesn't see anything. And then I drag myself over to the sink and I have to splash freezing cold water on my face, because by that point I'm usually sweating completely through my t-shirt. I'll look in the mirror, and my eyes are all watering and red, sometimes I get these little broken blood vessels around my eyelids, and I just look... exhausted. Just completely drained and gray. 

So when I walk out of that bathroom and head back down the hall to the elevators, it's not like I'm walking on air or feeling this great, positive sense of relief. doctor.question: Do you ever restrict your food intake to the point of significant weight loss or severe nutritional deficiency?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about restricting food intake leading to significant weight loss or nutritional deficiency, which is a symptom of Anorexia Nervosa. My symptom profile for Bulimia Nervosa does not include this symptom.

patient.answer:
I mean, no, not really. Not like... not like starving myself or anything like that. I don't think I've ever lost a bunch of weight all at once, or, you know, gotten sick from not eating enough vitamins or whatever you mean by nutritional deficiency. 

It's actually kind of the opposite problem, right? Like, I'm eating so much during those times when I lose control. But then, obviously, I'm trying to get rid of it. But in between all that... I do try to restrict what I eat, I really do. Like, I'll wake up after a bad night, after spending an hour in that library bathroom I told you about, and I'll just be so disgusted with myself. I'll look in the mirror in my dorm room—well, I try not to look, honestly, because I just hate what I see—but I'll tell myself, "Okay, today is the day. Today I'm only going to have black coffee and maybe an apple. I'm going to be perfectly controlled." 

And I'll try. I'll go to the dining hall and just get a salad with no dressing, and I'll sit there watching all the other guys on my floor eating burgers and fries, and it's just... it's torture. It's like my brain is just constantly buzzing with thoughts about food. I'll make it through the morning, maybe even the afternoon, just drinking water and trying to ignore how empty my stomach feels. But it never lasts long enough to actually make me lose weight or get deficient in anything. Because eventually, the hunger just gets too loud, or I get stressed about a paper, or I just feel so lonely and miserable, and then... then the whole cycle starts over again. I end up back in my room with a massive pile of food from the vending machines or the convenience store down the street. 

So, yeah, I try to restrict, I really try to be strict with myself to make up for the bad times, but I always end up failing. I never actually get to the point where I'm losing significant weight from it because the bingeing always ruins it. It's just this constant, exhausting back-and-forth, and my weight just kind of stays around the same, which honestly just makes me feel even worse because I feel like I'm doing all this awful stuff to my body and I'm not even getting the result I want, you know? It's just a mess.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's behavior is more characteristic of bulimia nervosa or anorexia nervosa, binge-eating/purging type
doctor.question: Do you ever experience a period of time where you don't binge eat or purge, but instead severely restrict your food intake for several days or weeks?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about periods of severe food restriction or fasting lasting for days or weeks (often to differentiate from Anorexia Nervosa or assess non-purging compensatory behaviors), which is not covered by my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
I mean... days or weeks? No. Definitely not. I wish I could, honestly, but no, I've never made it anywhere near that long. 

Like I was just saying a minute ago, I try to restrict. I really, really try. I'll make all these elaborate plans in my head. I'll even write it down in my planner sometimes, right next to my assignment due dates, like, "Monday: water only. Tuesday: one apple and black coffee." I build it up in my head like I'm finally going to take control, like I'm going to go on this long fast and completely reset my body and finally be disciplined. 

But it never, ever lasts for days. I think the absolute longest I've ever made it was maybe... I don't know, maybe 36 hours? And that was only because I had a massive history paper due and I basically locked myself in the library and drank about six energy drinks and just rode the caffeine anxiety until I crashed. But usually? I can barely make it 24 hours. 

It's just... the pressure builds up way too fast. I'll get to the evening of day one, and I'll be sitting in my dorm, trying to read for my intro to psych class or whatever, and the hunger just turns into this deafening static in my head. I can't focus on the words on the page. I can't watch a video. I can't even hold a normal conversation with my roommate because all I'm thinking about is the fact that I'm not eating, and then suddenly, all I can think about is everything I *want* to eat. 

It's like a pressure cooker, you know? I try to lock the lid down tight and tell myself I'm going to starve for a week, but the steam just builds and builds until I completely snap. By Monday night, I'm just pacing the room, listening to my roommate breathe while he sleeps, just waiting for the coast to be clear so I can sneak down to the vending machines in the basement or walk over to the 24-hour convenience store. 

So, no, I don't have these long stretches where I'm just severely restricting. I wish I had that kind of willpower, as messed up as that sounds. For me, the restricting is really just... it's just the waiting period between the binges. It's just the setup for the next failure. It never lasts more than a day or so before the whole awful cycle just explodes all over again.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's self-induced vomiting is aimed at compensating for the calories consumed during binge eating episodes
doctor.question: Is getting rid of the calories from the food you ate the primary reason you make yourself vomit after these episodes?

target_item.name: Compensatory_Behavior_Purging
target_item.manifestation: After I eat like that, I usually end up in a bathroom in the dorm or a quiet floor of the library making myself throw up because I feel terrified that the food is just sitting there turning into weight.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the primary motivation for vomiting (to get rid of calories/prevent weight gain), which aligns with the definition of inappropriate compensatory behaviors.

patient.answer:
Yeah, exactly. I know I kind of just went on a whole tangent about this a few minutes ago, but... yeah, that is absolutely the primary reason. It's the only reason, really. 

After I eat like that, when I've just totally lost all control and eaten everything in sight, I usually end up practically running to a bathroom—either the shared one in my dorm, if I can manage to sneak in without my roommate or any of the guys on my floor seeing me, or, you know, up on that super quiet floor of the library I was telling you about. I just have to get somewhere isolated as fast as humanly possible. 

And I'm in there making myself throw up purely because I feel... I just feel so completely terrified that the food is just sitting there. Like, I can physically feel it just sitting in my stomach like a massive, heavy brick, and my brain is just screaming at me that it's instantly turning into weight. It's this absolute, blinding panic that every second I wait, another calorie is being absorbed, and it's just attaching to my body and making me bigger. So getting rid of it, getting those calories out before they can actually turn into fat and change how I look... that's the whole point of doing it. It's the only thing that makes that terrified feeling stop.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's behavior is more characteristic of bulimia nervosa or anorexia nervosa, binge-eating/purging type
doctor.question: Do you currently have, or have you ever had, a period of time where you maintained a significantly low body weight for an extended period?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a history of significantly low body weight (a criterion for Anorexia Nervosa), which is not covered by my symptom profile for Bulimia Nervosa.

patient.answer:
No, never. And honestly, that’s the part that just... it drives me completely crazy. Like, I’ve never been significantly low weight, not ever. I’ve always just been... average. Or at least, I feel like I'm massive, but I guess on paper I'm just normal. When I was in middle school and early high school, I was maybe a little chubby, which I absolutely hated, and I thought when I came to college and started... well, doing all this, that I would finally get really thin. But it just hasn't happened. 

I actually have this digital scale that I bought at Target the second week of freshman year, and I keep it shoved way back under my bed in its original box so my roommate doesn't see it. I pull it out, like, every single morning when he goes to his 8 AM calc class. I strip down to nothing, make sure I've gone to the bathroom first, and I stand on it, just praying the number will be drastically lower. But it just... it just hovers right around the exact same five-pound range. It never drops into anything you'd call "significantly low." 

It’s so incredibly frustrating because I feel like I’m putting my body through a literal warzone, right? With the eating all that junk and then the panic and the throwing up in the library and then trying to starve myself the next day... you’d think—or at least I thought—that I’d have something to show for it. Like I’d be one of those guys who just looks incredibly lean and sharp, where my clothes just hang off me. But my jeans fit exactly the same as they did when my parents dropped me off in August. Sometimes they even feel tighter after a bad weekend, which just sends me into a total spiral of panic. 

So, no, I’ve never maintained a low weight. Not for a week, not for a month, never. My body just aggressively fights to stay right in the middle, which honestly makes me feel like such a massive failure. Like I can't even do this right. I'm doing all these extreme things, spending all my money on vending machine food, ruining my throat, and I just look like a completely regular, average guy to everyone else on campus. They have no idea what I'm doing behind closed doors because I don't look sick. It's like a sick joke, honestly. So yeah, definitely no extended periods of being really low weight. I wish, but no.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's behavior is more characteristic of bulimia nervosa or anorexia nervosa, binge-eating/purging type
doctor.question: Do you feel like you would still make yourself vomit after eating even if you weren't afraid of gaining weight?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking a hypothetical follow-up question to confirm that the sole motivation for purging is the fear of gaining weight. This specific hypothetical scenario is not covered in the symptom profile, as the patient's motivation for purging (to prevent weight gain) was already addressed in S048.

patient.answer:
I mean... no. I really don't think so. Honestly, I can't even wrap my head around that scenario because the fear of gaining weight is literally the entire reason I do it. Like, if I wasn't terrified of getting bigger, why on earth would I put myself through all of that? 

Making yourself throw up is completely miserable. It's not like it's a fun time, you know? My throat always burns afterward, my eyes get all puffy and bloodshot, and I constantly have this low-grade, nagging anxiety that someone in the dorm is going to hear me gagging or smell it on my breath when I walk back into my room. It's disgusting and it's so physically exhausting. 

If I could just eat whatever I wanted, like if I could just sit in the dining hall and eat five bowls of cereal and a whole pizza and know for an absolute fact that I wouldn't gain a single ounce... man, I would never go near a toilet again. I would just eat and then go back to my room and hang out or go to sleep like a normal person. 

The only reason I'm ever in that bathroom stall, practically suffocating myself to get everything up, is because the thought of my jeans not fitting or stepping on that digital scale under my bed and seeing the number go up by even half a pound just completely paralyzes me. Like I was saying before, the panic is entirely about the food turning into fat. It's not about anything else. If you somehow took that fear away, if I just magically didn't care what I looked like or how much I weighed, the throwing up would stop instantly. There just wouldn't be any point to it anymore. So, no, definitely not. It is one hundred percent about the weight.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's behavior is more aligned with bulimia nervosa or binge eating disorder
doctor.question: Do you typically feel a significant sense of relief after purging, which motivates you to continue this behavior?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the psychological feeling of relief after purging, which is a common clinical feature but does not map directly to any of the provided specific DSM-5 diagnostic criteria items in the symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Relief? I mean... I'm not really sure if 'relief' is the right word for it. And I definitely don't know if I'd say it's what motivates me to keep doing it. 

Like, I guess the immediate, blinding panic that I was talking about before—the fear of the calories—that part stops. But I wouldn't call what's left over a significant sense of relief. It's more like... well, let me just explain what happens right after, because it's really hard to put into words unless you're in it. 

When I finally finish up in that library bathroom, I'm usually kneeling there on these disgusting, freezing floor tiles, and my knees are aching, and my heart is just pounding out of my chest. I flush the toilet, usually like three or four times just to be absolutely, paranoid-level sure every single trace is gone so the janitor or whoever doesn't see anything. And then I drag myself over to the sink and I have to splash freezing cold water on my face, because by that point I'm usually sweating completely through my t-shirt. I'll look in the mirror, and my eyes are all watering and red, sometimes I get these little broken blood vessels around my eyelids, and I just look... exhausted. Just completely drained and gray. 

So when I walk out of that bathroom and head back down the hall to the elevators, it's not like I'm walking on air or feeling this great, positive sense of relief. I mostly just feel completely hollow. And cold. My throat is usually throbbing, my teeth feel weirdly sensitive, and I just have this overwhelming wave of guilt and shame wash over me that I actually let it happen again. I'm usually just dreading having to walk back into my dorm room and pretend to be totally fine and normal while my roommate is sitting right there playing Xbox. I have to somehow sit at my desk and focus on my calc homework when my brain feels like it's just made of static. 

So, no, I haven't really noticed a feeling of relief that makes me want to do it again. I'm really not sure what you mean by that, honestly, because if anything, the aftermath makes me swear to myself I'll never, ever do it again. I'll literally sit on my bed that night and promise myself, swear on my life, that it was the absolute last time, and tomorrow I'm just going to eat normally like a regular person. But then the next day comes, and I end up eating too much, and that exact same panic sets in all over again. So it's definitely not the aftermath that motivates me to keep going. The whole thing from start to finish is just... it's just miserable.
